Summary:
This paper reports a large-scale (>500 000 agents) empirical study that systematically tests >50 design and implementation choices for adversarial imitation learning (AIL) using both synthetic and human demonstration data. Its main finding is that algorithms tuned and evaluated only on synthetic (“artificial”) demonstrations often fail when confronted with human demonstrations, challenging a common evaluation practice in continuous-control imitation learning.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83]

Inference strategy justification:
The paper fragment explicitly links synthetic-only evaluation to poor real-world performance; all nodes and edges are therefore grounded directly in the reported findings. Moderate, clearly-marked inference was applied only to convert the paper’s recommendations (e.g. “synthetic demos are not a good proxy…”) into explicit AI-safety-relevant interventions such as “Collect diverse human demonstrations” and “Evaluate on human benchmarks”. Edge confidences are reduced (2–3) when such moderate inference is used.

Extraction completeness explanation:
All unique causal claims that connect the headline risk (“poor real-world performance of AIL policies”) to the recommended remedy (“use human demonstrations in training/evaluation”) are captured. Each intermediate reasoning step—from distributional mismatch, to the insight that representative data are needed, to the design decision of integrating human data, to the concrete empirical benchmarking mechanism, to the validation evidence—is modelled, producing an interconnected fabric with no disconnected nodes.

Key limitations:
1. Only the abstract was provided, so finer-grained section titles had to be approximated (e.g. “Abstract”).  
2. Additional detailed findings (e.g. which of the 50 choices mattered most) are likely contained in the full paper and are not extractable from the excerpt.  
3. Intervention maturity assessments are approximate because deployment status is not explicitly stated.
